newsitem.title: USA: Stocks end lower after defensive session.
newsitem.headline: Stocks end lower after defensive session.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks edged lower Friday as investors took a defensive stance in the next-to-last session of another solid year on Wall Street.

The Dow Jones industrial average ended down 11.54 points at 6,549.37 after spending much of the session higher. A late burst of computer-driven sell programmes erased the rally, thwarting the Dow's run at a second straight record.
The index of 30 blue-chip issues rose 14.23 points to a record 6,560.91 on Friday.

"Though it's hard to pick out a message from a day like today, it certainly seems the market has a defensive lean to it," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany. "It reflects a deepening concern that it's going to be tough to make money in the market next year."
The Dow actually spent most of the session modestly higher, boosted by strong performances from oil companies Chevron, Texaco and Exxon.
But a pair of late sell programmes slashed more than 42 points off the Dow in the last 35 minutes of trading, according to Birinyi Associates, a firm that tracks programme trading.
While the Dow ended lower, 1,402 stocks rose and 1,065 fell in the broader market on light New York Stock Exchange volume of 339 million shares.
Many investors took vacation this week because of the New Year's holiday on Wednesday.
At Monday's close with one session left in 1996, the Dow's gain for 1996 stood at a very strong 28 percent, especially since the blue-chip index rose 33.5 percent in 1995.
While much of the market was quiet, a small group of computer service stocks saw hectic, volatile trading.

At the centre of the frenzy is a glitch in many major corporate computer systems that leaves them unprepared to process dates as of the year 2000. A number of small companies devoted to solving the problem were bid sharply higher early in the session, only to beat a hasty retreat late in the day.
Among them were TSR Inc., which fell 7-1/2 to 30 after trading as high as 50-1/4. Acceler8 Technology fell 5-1/8 to 16-3/8 after peaking at 30-5/8.

But the most dramatic move came from Zitel Corp., which plunged 20-1/4 to 41 after hitting 72-7/8 earlier in the session. More than 11.1 million shares changed hands, making it the most active issue on Nasdaq.
Zitel had surged last week on optimism about its stake in a company that specialises in the year 2000 bug and on rumours financier George Soros was considering buying a stake.
But a source close to Soros Fund Management said late Monday that no such investment was planned.
The episode had the whiff of market mania, analysts said.

"This was like the biotech craze of 1991, only faster," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. "There may still be some interest in these stocks later, but this was a bubble that got way out of control."
In other issues, Long Island Lighting rose 2-5/8 to 22 a day after announcing it would merge with Brooklyn Union Gas Co. to create a $4 billion utility company. Brooklyn Union shares fell 3/4 to 30.
Marks Brothers Jewellers Inc. slid 8-1/4 to 13-1/4 after Montgomery Securities cut its fourth quarter earnings estimate on the company.
The Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks fell 2.94 points to 753.85.
The Nasdaq composite index, laden with high-technology issues, fell 3.63 to 1,287.75.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 0.68 point to 397.42. The average share fell 7 cents.
The American Stock Exchange index edged up 1.53 to 583.46.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,274.203, down 14.653 points, or 0.2 percent.
